Technical mechanics

Mechanical drive design calculation

Interactive teaching guide · AutoMethod v0.4.11 · 2026

Lomakin V. O.; Melnychuk S. V.

The guide covers both load input methods, cylindrical, bevel, worm, planetary and combined stages, no flexible transmission, belt, timing belt and chain options, and component checks. Numerical substitutions are a teaching example calculated by native engdoc; they do not replace the assigned task.

All equations are evaluated in SI. Speed n is in s⁻¹; \(n_{\mathrm{min}^{-1}}=60n_{\mathrm{s}^{-1}}\). Stress is given in Pa and MPa, life in seconds and hours. This general guide covers alternatives; the report at the end of the interactive page contains only the selected current variant.

1. Task and inputs

First define the working-machine load and input method. Notation and initial relations follow below. Construction sizing runs in a background worker; parameter changes cancel stale requests. If a restored variant needs larger shafts and bearings, compatible dimensions are coordinated automatically. The initial variant becomes the comparison baseline if none exists; load, material and allowable stresses remain unchanged. Reload restores the saved variant. “Open verified example” first downloads a backup JSON. Save the task before changing construction.

Required torque \(T'_{3}\) and speed \(n'_{3}\) of the working shaft define required power:

\[P'_{3}=2\pi T'_{3}n'_{3}\]
(1.1)

For tangential-force input \(F\) and linear speed \(v\) use the working diameter \(D\) of the driven element:

\[P'_{3}=Fv\]
(1.2)
\[n'_{3}=\frac{v}{\pi D}\]
(1.3)

Equations use s⁻¹; fields use min⁻¹. Permissible relative speed deviation is denoted \(\varepsilon\); actual deviation — \(\delta_n\). For a tolerance of 5%, the permitted range is −5% to +5%. Dimensions, efficiencies and safety factors are adopted for the task. Stock material and SKF bearings can be selected from the shared catalogues. Do not apply a safety factor again to an already allowable stress. Motor power is its mechanical shaft power. Displayed numbers use five significant figures; calculations and saved data retain full precision.

Shaft, gear and ratio notation

Shafts are numbered from the gearbox input. On the intermediate shaft, the second index distinguishes the first-stage wheel from the second-stage pinion. For planetary stages, s denotes the sun, p the planet and r the fixed ring; w denotes the number of worm starts. A prime denotes a desired value, for example \(u'_1\); without a prime — the adopted value \(u_1\). Iterations are numbered separately.

Table 1.1 — Shafts and quantity notation
ShaftGear elementsPowerSpeedTorque
1 · input\(z_{1}\)\(P_{1}\)\(n_{1}\)\(T_{1}\)
2 · intermediate\(z_{2\text{-}1}\); \(z_{2\text{-}2}\)\(P_{2}\)\(n_{2}\)\(T_{2}\)
3 · output\(z_{3}\)\(P_{3}\)\(n_{3}\)\(T_{3}\)

\(u\) — gearbox reduction ratio, \(u_{\mathrm e}\) — for the belt or chain, \(u_{\Sigma}\) — overall drive ratio; m denotes the motor:

\[u=u_{1}\,u_{2}=\frac{n_1}{n_{3}}\]
(1.4)
\[u_{\Sigma}=u_{\mathrm e}u=\frac{n_{\mathrm m}}{n_{3}}\]
(1.5)

2. Kinematics, power and torque

KNUBA guides: gearbox gear stage 3…6, chain 2…6, conventional belt up to 4, single-start worm 28…80, two-start worm 14…40 (p. 14, table 4). Extended teaching search ranges: cylindrical 2…8, bevel 2…5, planetary 3…8, four-start worm 8…20. Allocate more reduction to the worm stage. Automatic mode selects all stages; editing desired u or teeth enables manual mode. Recommendations and acceptance buttons are directly below the fields in section 2. Overall drive ratio is uΣ, gearbox ratio is u. With unequal modules, equal stage ratios do not mean equal diameters; equations (2.1)–(2.2) give the geometric guide. Interactive selection compares integer teeth and envelopes while preserving the task, motor, modules and widths. This is a teaching compactness criterion; strength and bearing checks must follow. Select one or two stages and the transmission before the gearbox. Adopt integer tooth counts, then check actual output speed within ±ε. If it fails, adjust teeth and repeat kinematic and load calculations before adopting dimensions. Resolve insufficient power or torque by selecting a motor for its duty.

Table 2.1 — Parameters and adoption
ParameterTeaching value / alternatives
Motor mechanical power \(P_{\mathrm m}\)2,2 kW
Mechanical shaft power. Select a rating from the ABB reference series or enter your own nameplate data.
Motor operating speed \(n_{\mathrm m}\)1 440 min⁻¹
Nameplate speed under load. Select a variant for the adopted power or enter custom data.
Ratio allocation \(q_{split}\)Automatic allocation by type and dimensions; Manual allocation; apply the proposal below
Automatic: allocate all stages by dimensions and speed. Editing a desired ratio or tooth count enables manual mode.
Desired belt / chain ratio \(u'_{\mathrm e}\)2
Guide: conventional belt 2…4; chain 2…6. Timing belt search guide 2…6; check minimum teeth, wrap and product rating. These are not hard limits; editing enables manual mode.
Desired first-stage ratio \(u'_1\)4
Planetary guide: 3…8, u = 1 + zᵣ/zₛ with fixed ring and carrier output; tooth counts and planet count must permit assembly. Cylindrical stage: start with 3…6, extended search guide 2…8; bevel 2…5. Worm: single-start 28…80, two-start 14…40; four-start teaching guide 8…20. Overall drive ratio comes from motor and specified output speed and is allocated between the external transmission and gearbox. Similar ratios give similar diameters only with compatible modules, pinion tooth counts and helix angles; allocate more reduction to the worm stage. The recommendation below accounts for type and size; check modules, widths, strength and bearings after allocation.

For two cylindrical stages with similar modules, pinion tooth counts and helix angles, the initial allocation is:

\[u_1\approx u_2\approx\sqrt{u}\]
(2.1)

For different geometries, a guide to similar gear diameters is:

\[u_1\approx\sqrt{u\,\frac{m_{\mathrm n,2}z_{2\text{-}2}/\cos\beta_2}{m_{\mathrm n,1}z_1/\cos\beta_1}}\]
(2.2)

3. Belts, timing belts and chains

For a V-belt drive, select a classical Z/A/B/C/D/E or narrow SPZ/SPA/SPB/SPC section from the shared Optibelt CSV. Check minimum pulley datum diameters; do not mix Li and Ld designations. Use the compactness recommendation in section 2 for ratio allocation, then check loads and bearings. The “No flexible transmission” option omits this section from the interactive calculation and report: \(u_{\mathrm e}=\eta_{\mathrm e}=1\). A conventional belt includes slip and span tensions; a timing belt uses a compatible profile, pitch, width and tooth count; a chain uses a compatible pitch, integer sprocket tooth counts and an even number of links. All three alternatives appear below. Enter belt or chain working ratings for the specific product; breaking force is not a permissible working load.

Table 3.1 — Parameters and adoption
ParameterTeaching value / alternatives
Driving pulley datum diameter \(d_{b1}\)100 mm

4. Gear drives

Select the gearbox type in section 1. A cylindrical stage has \(\beta=0^\circ\) for spur teeth or \(\beta>0^\circ\) for helical teeth; mating gears have opposite helix hands. Specify shaft angle for bevel gears, starts and q in the normal system for worm gears, and sun, planets and planet count for planetary gears. Combined permits different stage types. Selection determines kinematics and geometry; noncylindrical product strength is checked against its stated torque rating. Planetary stage: fixed ring, sun input, carrier output; \(u_j=1+\frac{z_{\mathrm r,j}}{z_{\mathrm s,j}}\). Conditions: \(z_{\mathrm r,j}=z_{\mathrm s,j}+2z_{\mathrm p,j}\); \(\frac{z_{\mathrm s,j}+z_{\mathrm r,j}}{N_j}\) is an integer; \(z_{\mathrm p,j}+2<(z_{\mathrm s,j}+z_{\mathrm p,j})\sin(\pi/N_j)\). Size comparison uses the ring outer envelope including internal tooth roots and rim thickness. Select a module from the first reference series; second-series or custom values require tooling and availability justification. This model uses the conservative limit z ≥ 18. Index z₁₋₁ denotes the first-stage pinion and z₂₋₂ the second-stage gear. Involute flanks and face width form the 3D view geometry. The root transition fillet is approximate; the view is not a manufacturing drawing.

Select teaching assumptions for material, heat treatment, fits, accuracy grade, surface texture, geometric tolerances and hubs in section 4. Hub dimensions, induction hardening depth and tooth thickness reduction are in the collapsed fields. These requirements are saved in JSON and do not change strength calculation allowables. Gear datum A is the bore axis and B is the hub abutment face; shaft journal axes form common datum A–B. Ra, runout and perpendicularity are adopted manufacturing requirements. Cylindrical gears reference ISO 1328-1, bevel gears ISO 17485 and worm gears DIN 3974. Construction conflicts are shown before export; the nominal outline is not a toolpath.

5. Tooth bending and contact

The specified factor K is applied once. Tooth allowable stresses and form factors depend on material, surface condition and life; they cannot be equated to steel yield strength. The Hertz estimate describes local elastic contact at the pitch point. Full contact and bending fatigue assessments require additional ISO 6336 factors.

0 — no rating specified. Adopt the rating of an actual product for the material, speed, life and service conditions; teaching geometry alone does not determine load capacity.
Stage 2: nameplate / catalogue torque rating \(T_{rating2}\)0 N·m

Stage 2: pinion diameter, m.
\(d_{3}\)
Stage 2: wheel diameter, m.

(5.13)
\[\rho_2 = \frac{\sin\left(0{,}349066\right)\cdot0{,}08\cdot0{,}276}{\left(2\cdot\left(0{,}08+0{,}276\right)\right)} = 0{,}010606\;\text{m} = 10{,}606\;\text{mm}\](5.13a)

For stage 2. Local Hertz contact pressure is estimated for elastic steel surfaces. This estimate does not replace a full ISO 6336 calculation. [2]

\(p_{H2}\)
Stage 2: local Hertz pressure, MPa.
\(E\)
Steel Young's modulus, Pa.
\(F_{t2}\)
Stage 2: tangential force, N.
\(K\)
Design load factor, dimensionless.
\(\alpha_{t2}\)
Stage 2: transverse pressure angle, dimensionless.
\(b_{2}\)
Stage 2: face width, m.
\(\nu\)
Poisson's ratio, dimensionless.
\(\pi\)
number π, dimensionless.
\(\rho_2\)
Stage 2: reduced curvature radius, m.
\[p_{H2} = \sqrt{\frac{ {F_{t2}}\cdot{K}\cdot {E}}{\left(2\cdot\left(1-{{\nu}}^{2}\right)\cdot{\pi}\cdot {b_{2}}\cdot {\rho_2}\cdot\cos\left( {\alpha_{t2}}\right)\right)}}\]
(5.14)

6. Low-speed shaft

Place the gear between bearings A and B. The tangential and radial load resultant defines the diagram plane. Before the gear Q = \(R_{A}\), after it Q = −\(R_{B}\); the Q jump is −F. Bending moment is continuous and zero at the bearings; its slope equals Q. Select material by grade, condition and original stock diameter. Adopt minimum static safety factor n and check \(\sigma_{\mathrm{eq}}\le R_{\mathrm e}/[n]\). Also check deflection and twist. Fatigue and stress concentrations need separate assessment.

7. Rolling bearings

When opening an incompatible variant or exporting A1, compatible output shaft, hub, coupling and bearing dimensions are coordinated automatically. Both A1 buttons complete sizing and drawing in one click. If the journal is too small, “Select output shaft and bearings” in section 7 prepares a separate dimensional proposal with keys and mounting approach; accept it after reviewing the changes table. Selection also checks actual stepped sections; other failed conditions are shown separately. Select an open SKF ball bearing from the shared CSV or enter data for a specific custom product. Saved C, C₀, bore and limiting speed must refer to one variant. Spur meshing has no axial force, so \(P=R\). L₁₀ life corresponds to 90% reliability. Check both bearings, nominal bore and limiting speed; adopt lubrication, clearances, fits and modified life separately.

Check the bearing journal using design torque and axial force with the adopted stress concentration factor. Bending moment is zero at the ideal support centre; other sections and overhangs need additional checks. [4]

\[\sigma_{eq,j} = {K_{j}}\cdot\sqrt{{\left(\frac{4\cdot {F_{a,out}}}{\left({\pi}\cdot{ {d_{j}}}^{2}\right)}\right)}^{2}+3\cdot{\left(\frac{16\cdot {T_d}}{\left({\pi}\cdot{ {d_{j}}}^{3}\right)}\right)}^{2}}\]
(7.1)

Shaft, bearing and hub design

First define assembly order and axial force paths, then specify shoulders and fits. Fit, torque transmission and axial retention are separate requirements.

Table 7.2 — Construction design rules
ElementWhat to determine
Mounting and dismountingEach part must pass from a free end to its seat. Provide a smaller diameter before the seating journal and puller access. ⌀39 h6 before ⌀40 k6 is a teaching example. The editable 1 mm step is not a universal rule.
Datums and dimensionsThe output shaft journal axes establish common datum A–B. For the gear, A is the bore axis and B is the hub abutment face. Dimension axial positions from a functional stop; check the dimension chain, seat runout and face perpendicularity.
Fits and surface textureSelect tolerance zones for ring rotation relative to the load, temperature and duty. Journal k6 and gear bore H7 are teaching assumptions. Clearance along the mounting path does not loosen the working fit. Specify Ra and geometric tolerances for each functional surface.
Shoulders, fillets and chamfersObtain the abutment diameter dₐ and permissible radius rₐ for the selected bearing. The fillet must clear the ring face; a larger radius requires a compatible spacer. An entry chamfer facilitates assembly. R1 and 1 × 45° are editable assumptions here, not catalogue limits.
Manufacturing relief groovesUse a relief groove per ISO 18388 for tool or grinding-wheel clearance only where machining requires it. Do not confuse it with a retaining-ring groove. Grooves, threads and keyways reduce the section and require strength and fatigue checks.
Bearing axial locationIdentify the locating and floating bearings. Restrain both rings of the locating bearing axially in both directions. Options include a shoulder and nut with a lock washer, an end plate or an approved retaining ring; a thread is needed only for the selected method. The floating arrangement must allow thermal expansion.
Gears, pulleys and couplingsThe key transmits torque; define hub axial stops in both directions separately. Coordinate shoulder, spacer and nut or end plate with hub width, assembly direction and axial force. For a bevel pair, the abutment face position determines mounting distance and meshing. All rings, sleeves and fasteners must appear in the assembly and BOM.

Sources: NTN: mounting, fits and abutments; SKF: Maintenance handbook, pp. 37–38; KG: gear retention, pp. 51–53; ISO 5459:2024 — datums; ISO 18388:2016 — relief grooves.

The shared construction model defines collars, removable stepped sleeves, hubs, end plates, M10 axial bolts, covers and seals. Parts share identifiers across the assembly, BOM, drawings and assembly sequence. Mounting paths, axial positioning and individual shaft sections are checked. Covers and seal envelopes are teaching dimensions; tightening, locking, fatigue and final seal selection require product-specific checks.

8. Key and output coupling

Select key dimensions for the specific shaft diameter and hub. A round-ended key has effective length l − b. Check bearing stress and shear separately. Compare coupling design torque with the product rating for the adopted duty; do not increase the rating without selecting another product.

9. Bolted joint

Specify external load, bolt count, preload and load fraction χ according to joint stiffness. First check residual joint compression. After separation, results from the linear χ model do not establish serviceability. Friction resists slip; shank shear is a separate assessment after slip. Threads in the shear plane, bearing stress, eccentricity and tightening scatter require additional checks.

Stress after slip: shank shear, Pa.
\[\sigma_{eq,bolt} = \sqrt{{ {\sigma_{b,bolt}}}^{2}+3\cdot{ {\tau_b}}^{2}}\]
(9.7)
\[\sigma_{eq,bolt} = \sqrt{{1{,}25792\cdot10^{+8}}^{2}+3\cdot{8{,}84194\cdot10^{+6}}^{2}} = 126720000\;\text{Pa} = 126{,}72\;\text{MPa}\](9.7a)

Estimate tightening torque using the adopted factor Kₜ. Account separately for friction and tool accuracy scatter. [38]

\(M_A\)
Approximate tightening torque, N·m.
\(F_{pre}\)
Preload per bolt, N.
\(K_{T}\)
Approximate tightening factor, dimensionless.
\(d_{bolt}\)
Nominal bolt diameter, m.
\[M_A = {K_{T}}\cdot {F_{pre}}\cdot {d_{bolt}}\]
(9.8)
\[M_A = 0{,}2\cdot10000\cdot0{,}012 = 24\;\text{N·m}\](9.8a)

10. Basic machine-element calculations

The rod and spring are separate examples, not drive loads. The rod uses linear elasticity. Adopt the physical material limit and required safety factor \([n]>1\): \([\sigma]=R_{\mathrm e}/[n]\), \(n=R_{\mathrm e}/\sigma\ge[n]\). The spring similarly uses its limiting shear stress. Do not apply a second safety factor to an already specified allowable stress. Teaching values [n] = 2 and 1.5 require justification for the duty; they are not universal requirements. Use \(D/d\ge4\) and spring-wire properties for the spring. Check stress with curvature correction, rate and working travel; coil contact, buckling and fatigue are not calculated here.

Table 10.1 — Parameters and adoption
ParameterTeaching value / alternatives
Rod axial force \(F_{rod}\)10 kN
Rod cross-sectional area \(A_{rod}\)100 mm²
Rod length \(L_{rod}\)500 mm
Strength limit input method \(q_{basic}\)Ready-made allowable stresses (without a physical safety factor); Material strength limits and required safety factor
Adopted rod material yield strength \(R_{rod}\)300 MPa
300 MPa is an adopted teaching value; use the verified yield strength for the actual material condition and size.
Required rod safety factor [n] \(n_{rod}\)2
Adopted static tensile minimum; [σ] = Rₑ/[n]. The value 2 is a teaching choice, not a universal requirement for all materials.
Wire-material limiting shear stress \(R_{sp}\)600 MPa
600 MPa is a teaching assumption. A verified wire-material limit and failure criterion are required; fatigue life is checked separately.
Required spring safety factor [n] \(n_{sp}\)1,5
Adopted minimum based on limiting shear stress; [τ] = τ_lim/[n]. Fatigue requires separate data.
Allowable rod stress \(S_{rod}\)160 MPa
Spring force \(F_{sp}\)100 N
Spring wire diameter \(d_{w}\)4 mm
Mean spring diameter \(D_{sp}\)30 mm
Active coils \(N_{sp}\)8
Allowable wire stress \(\tau_{sp}\)400 MPa
Spring travel / wheel travel ratio \(i_{motion}\)0,8

Axial tensile stress uses a uniformly loaded rod of constant cross-section. [2]

\(\sigma_{rod}\)
Axial tensile stress, MPa.
\(A_{rod}\)
Rod cross-sectional area, m².
\(F_{rod}\)
Rod axial force, N.
\[\sigma_{rod} = \frac{ {F_{rod}}}{ {A_{rod}}}\]
(10.1)
\[\sigma_{rod} = \frac{10000}{1\cdot10^{-4}} = 100000000\;\text{Pa} = 100\;\text{MPa}\](10.1a)

Use the entered allowable stress or calculate it from yield strength and the required static safety factor. [40]

\([\sigma]_{rod}\)
Allowable rod stress, MPa.
\(R_{rod}\)
Adopted rod material yield strength, Pa.
\(n_{rod}\)
Required rod safety factor [n], dimensionless.
\[[\sigma]_{rod} = \frac{ {R_{rod}}}{ {n_{rod}}}\]
(10.2)
\[[\sigma]_{rod} = \frac{3\cdot10^{+8}}{2} = 150000000\;\text{Pa} = 150\;\text{MPa}\](10.2a)

Actual yield safety factor uses the verified or explicitly adopted material limit; compare with required [n] > 1. [40]

\(n_{rod}\)
Actual rod safety factor, dimensionless.
\(R_{rod}\)
Adopted rod material yield strength, Pa.
\(\sigma_{rod}\)
Axial tensile stress, Pa.
\[n_{rod} = \frac{ {R_{rod}}}{ {\sigma_{rod}}}\]
(10.3)
\[n_{rod} = \frac{3\cdot10^{+8}}{1\cdot10^{+8}} = 3\](10.3a)

Strain follows Hooke's law within the linear-elastic range. [2]

\(\varepsilon_{rod}\)
Rod strain, dimensionless.
\(E\)
Steel Young's modulus, Pa.
\(\sigma_{rod}\)
Axial tensile stress, Pa.
\[\varepsilon_{rod} = \frac{ {\sigma_{rod}}}{ {E}}\]
(10.4)
\[\varepsilon_{rod} = \frac{1\cdot10^{+8}}{2{,}1\cdot10^{+11}} = 0{,}00047619\](10.4a)

Rod elongation is determined from its force, length and axial stiffness EA. [2]

\(\Delta L_{rod}\)
Rod extension, mm.
\(A_{rod}\)
Rod cross-sectional area, m².
\(E\)
Steel Young's modulus, Pa.
\(F_{rod}\)
Rod axial force, N.
\(L_{rod}\)
Rod length, m.
\[\Delta L_{rod} = \frac{ {F_{rod}}\cdot {L_{rod}}}{\left( {E}\cdot {A_{rod}}\right)}\]
(10.5)
\[\Delta L_{rod} = \frac{10000\cdot0{,}5}{\left(2{,}1\cdot10^{+11}\cdot1\cdot10^{-4}\right)} = 0{,}0002381\;\text{m} = 0{,}2381\;\text{mm}\](10.5a)

Spring index is mean coil diameter divided by wire diameter; this model requires an index of at least 4. [41]

\(c_{sp}\)
Spring index, dimensionless.
\(D_{sp}\)
Mean spring diameter, m.
\(d_{w}\)
Spring wire diameter, m.
\[c_{sp} = \frac{ {D_{sp}}}{ {d_{w}}}\]
(10.6)
\[c_{sp} = \frac{0{,}03}{0{,}004} = 7{,}5\](10.6a)

The wire curvature factor uses Chassis Handbook equation 3.57; it corrects stress relative to a straight rod. [41]

\(k_{\tau,sp}\)
Wire curvature factor, dimensionless.
\(c_{sp}\)
Spring index, dimensionless.
\[k_{\tau,sp} = \frac{\left( {c_{sp}}+0.5\right)}{\left( {c_{sp}}-0.75\right)}\]
(10.7)
\[k_{\tau,sp} = \frac{\left(7{,}5+0{,}5\right)}{\left(7{,}5-0{,}75\right)} = 1{,}1852\](10.7a)

The cylindrical spring rate uses round wire and the specified active coil count. [41]

\(k_{sp}\)
Spring rate, N/mm.
\(D_{sp}\)
Mean spring diameter, m.
\(G\)
Shear modulus, Pa.
\(N_{sp}\)
Active coils, dimensionless.
\(d_{w}\)
Spring wire diameter, m.
\[k_{sp} = \frac{ {G}\cdot{ {d_{w}}}^{4}}{\left(8\cdot{ {D_{sp}}}^{3}\cdot {N_{sp}}\right)}\]
(10.8)
\[k_{sp} = \frac{8{,}07692\cdot10^{+10}\cdot{0{,}004}^{4}}{\left(8\cdot{0{,}03}^{3}\cdot8\right)} = 11966\;\text{N/m} = 11{,}966\;\text{N/mm}\](10.8a)

Working deflection follows from linear stiffness at the specified working force. [41]

\(f_{sp}\)
Spring working deflection, mm.
\(F_{sp}\)
Spring force, N.
\(k_{sp}\)
Spring rate, N/m.
\[f_{sp} = \frac{ {F_{sp}}}{ {k_{sp}}}\]
(10.9)
\[f_{sp} = \frac{100}{11965{,}8} = 0{,}0083571\;\text{m} = 8{,}3571\;\text{mm}\](10.9a)

Wire shear stress includes curvature correction. Check coil contact and fatigue life separately. [41]

\(\tau_{sp}\)
Wire shear stress, MPa.
\(D_{sp}\)
Mean spring diameter, m.
\(F_{sp}\)
Spring force, N.
\(k_{\tau,sp}\)
Wire curvature factor, dimensionless.
\(d_{w}\)
Spring wire diameter, m.
\(\pi\)
number π, dimensionless.
\[\tau_{sp} = \frac{ {k_{\tau,sp}}\cdot8\cdot {F_{sp}}\cdot {D_{sp}}}{\left({\pi}\cdot{ {d_{w}}}^{3}\right)}\]
(10.10)
\[\tau_{sp} = \frac{1{,}18519\cdot8\cdot100\cdot0{,}03}{\left(3{,}14159\cdot{0{,}004}^{3}\right)} = 141470000\;\text{Pa} = 141{,}47\;\text{MPa}\](10.10a)

Use the entered allowable shear stress or calculate it from the material limit and required safety factor. [40]

\([\tau]_{sp}\)
Allowable wire shear stress, MPa.
\(R_{sp}\)
Wire-material limiting shear stress, Pa.

\[[\tau]_{sp} = \frac{ {R_{sp}}}{ {n_{sp}}}\]
(10.11)

\(n_{sp}\)
Actual spring safety factor, dimensionless.
\(R_{sp}\)

\(\tau_{sp}\)

Strain energy is the area under the linear spring force–deflection curve. [41]

\(W_{sp}\)
Spring strain energy, J.
\(F_{sp}\)
Spring force, N.
\(f_{sp}\)

11. Comparison and design justification

Save a baseline with the same working-machine requirements. “Prepare construction refinement” shows the initial failed condition, adopted change and repeated calculations. Acceptance updates the fields and saves the sequence in JSON and PDF. If no catalogue solution exists, the condition remains failed. State the selection reason, limit comparison, actual safety factor and model limitations in the conclusion.

Appendix. Verified teaching examples

With the same requirements \(T=200\;\text{N·m}\), \(n=76{,}394\;\text{min}^{-1}\) and a 2.2 kW / 1440 min⁻¹ motor, the flexible transmission changes gearbox input speed. Automatic selection refines the allocation between both stages and the flexible transmission; all other changes require a repeated check.
